item.title: authn-revokd
item.description:
OpenSSH has no way to distribute a KRL, and nothing in a KRL says it is stale. sshd reads a file that stopped updating months ago as the current list. authn-revokd closes both gaps for the lists authn-bridge publishes: it fetches each list, keeps it only if it verifies, writes it where sshd or a TLS server reads it, and, when a list lapses, writes one that revokes the CA itself. Pure Go, CGO_ENABLED=0, one binary. These pages describe v0.6.2.

$ go install github.com/go-authn/revocation/cmd/authn-revokd@v0.6.2
$ authn-revokd -version
authn-revokd v0.6.2
$ authn-revokd -help
Usage of authn-revokd:
-config string
the configuration file (default "/etc/authn-revokd/revokd.hcl")
-once
sync once and exit: 1 when a list is not current, or could not be fetched
-version
print the version and exit

-help exits 0; before v0.6.2 it exited 2.

Before v0.6.0 the command was revokd, and read /etc/revokd.hcl by default. Nothing reads that file any more; when it is there and the new default is not, the error names both paths.

What it does, in one run

Against a test authn-bridge on loopback, with a KRL source and a CRL source:

$ authn-revokd -config revokd.hcl -once
bridge-ssh: version 0, issued 2026-10-10T20:57:59Z, expires 2026-10-10T21:57:59Z
bridge-x509: version 1791665879411, issued 2026-10-10T20:57:59Z, expires 2026-10-10T21:57:59Z
output sshd: wrote /tmp/docs-patch-a2daf7c8/revokd/out/sshd.krl
output tls: wrote /tmp/docs-patch-a2daf7c8/revokd/out/bridge.crl
$ ssh-keygen -Q -l -f out/sshd.krl
# KRL version 0
# Generated at 20261010T225759
# Comment: authn-revokd sshd

A second run with nothing new prints nothing and exits 0: an output is rewritten only when its content changes.

Why the transport does not matter

Every list authenticates itself: a KRL by a detached SSHSIG signature by the CA’s own key, a CRL by its CA’s signature. Every list says when it stops being current. So a list may come over HTTPS, plain HTTP inside a cluster, a mirror, or a file. The transport decides how fast a change arrives, never whether a forged or stale list is taken.

KRL CRL
authentic SSHSIG by the SSH CA key, namespace krl@go-authn.github.io signed by its CA
current expires@go-authn.github.io, which sshd ignores nextUpdate
never backwards krl_version, then generation date CRL Number, then thisUpdate
fail closed authn-revokd writes a KRL that revokes the CA key OpenSSL refuses an expired CRL by itself

Where to go next

Installing it the daemon, or -once on a timer; wiring sshd and nginx
The configuration sources, outputs, the mirror, and what is refused
How a list is verified signature, dates, and never older than the list held, across restarts
When a list lapses the KRL that revokes the CA itself

What it does not do

A revocation reaches a server no faster than authn-revokd polls (refresh), plus the issuer’s delay in issuing again. While the issuer is down, its certificates are refused from the list’s expiry on. Whoever holds a CA’s key can sign any list, as they can sign any certificate.

Licence

BSD-3-Clause.

item.title: How a list is verified
item.description:
A list that does not verify is never written, served or used. The last good copy stays. A fetch that fails, for any reason, never replaces it with an empty answer, which would revoke nothing.

The signature

A KRL is fetched with its signature, <url>.sig: an armored SSHSIG over the whole file, by the SSH CA key configured as ssh_ca, in the namespace krl@go-authn.github.io. The namespace keeps the signature from being taken for anything else. A signer hashes with SHA-512; SHA-256 is accepted too. An RSA signature in the SHA-1 form, which PROTOCOL.sshsig forbids, is refused.

The KRL itself must parse as sshd parses it, and must not carry OpenSSH’s own signature section, which OpenSSH never verifies.

A list signed by any other key is refused:

$ authn-revokd -config revokd-other.hcl -once
bridge-ssh: revocation: the KRL's signature does not verify by SHA256:SLbG7N+YZ/TQ6B3I1DQLYo2/6In4OWx5GYkRfKIxpxo: public key does not match
bridge-x509: version 1791665695047, issued 2026-10-10T20:54:55Z, expires 2026-10-10T21:54:55Z
output sshd: wrote /tmp/docs-patch-a2daf7c8/revokd/out/other.krl
output tls: wrote /tmp/docs-patch-a2daf7c8/revokd/out/other.crl
authn-revokd: not current: bridge-ssh

Here ssh_ca named a key that did not sign bridge’s list, and the error names that key. A signature that does not verify may also be a list issued again between the two requests, so both are fetched once more before it is reported. This was the first fetch of that source, so there was no good copy to keep, and the output is the fail-closed list at once. (Before v0.6.2 the same failure was reported as “the list changed between it and its signature”, ahead of the same words.)

The signature is fetched with If-Match: <the list's ETag>. A list issued again between the two requests answers 412, and both are fetched again.

A CRL is checked against the CA certificate configured as x509_ca: its signature first, on the raw bytes, before the rest is parsed, so a large CRL signed by anybody costs a signature check rather than a parse. Then its issuer must be that certificate’s subject; it must have a CRL Number and a nextUpdate after its thisUpdate; and it must not be a delta CRL, nor carry a critical extension other than the CRL Number and the Authority Key Identifier, nor a critical entry extension.

A KRL must also say when it expires, in the expires@go-authn.github.io extension: one that does not could never be told from a stale one.

Bodies are bounded: a KRL at 32 MiB, its signature at 64 KiB, a CRL at 64 MiB.

The dates

A list is current when:

  • now is before its expiry (the KRL’s extension, the CRL’s nextUpdate);
  • it was not issued more than five minutes in the future: an issuer whose clock is ahead by more than that writes lists whose age cannot be known;
  • with max_age, it was issued no longer ago than that.

A list that is not current is refused when fetched. A 304 Not Modified is no news: the copy held may have expired since, and it is judged again at every sync.

Never older than the list held

A list’s position is its version (the KRL’s krl_version, the CRL Number), then its issue time (the KRL’s generation date, the CRL’s thisUpdate). A list may replace the one held only when it has a higher version, or the same version issued later: the same revocations, issued again with a new expiry. Anything else is a rollback: a replayed or restored older list, still signed and unexpired, that would un-revoke what the newer one revoked.

Across restarts too

The list held is kept in state_dir, one file per source holding the list and its signature together, written by a single rename with the directory synced. At start each copy is verified again (expired or not, it orders what comes next), and a copy that no longer verifies is not trusted, not even to order the next one, and is said so in the log.

Here a source is pointed, after a restart, at a list an earlier bridge process served fourteen seconds before, still signed and still unexpired:

$ authn-revokd -config revokd.hcl -once
bridge-ssh: version 0, issued 2026-10-10T20:54:50Z, expires 2026-10-10T21:54:50Z
bridge-x509: version 1791665695047, issued 2026-10-10T20:54:55Z, expires 2026-10-10T21:54:55Z
output sshd: wrote /tmp/docs-patch-a2daf7c8/revokd/out/sshd.krl
output tls: wrote /tmp/docs-patch-a2daf7c8/revokd/out/bridge.crl
$ authn-revokd -config revokd-old.hcl -once
bridge-ssh: file:///tmp/docs-patch-a2daf7c8/revokd/old/bridge.krl: revocation: the list is older than the one held: version 0 issued at 2026-10-10T20:54:36Z, the copy held at 2026-10-10T20:54:50Z
authn-revokd: not fetched: bridge-ssh (the list held is current until 2026-10-10T21:54:50Z)
$ ssh-keygen -Q -l -f out/sshd.krl
# KRL version 0
# Generated at 20261010T225450
# Comment: authn-revokd sshd

The older list is refused and the output keeps the newer one. The process that refused it had never seen the newer list: it read it back from state_dir.

Since the state is what makes a rollback detectable, the directory is held to sshd’s StrictModes rule (the configuration). A crash between two writes cannot leave a pair that fails to verify, which would take the rollback guard with it: the list and its signature are one file.

What -once reports

-once exits 1 when a source has no current list, when its last fetch failed, or when an output could not be written, and its last line says which of the first two it is:

last line the source its outputs
not current: <source> holds no current list: never fetched, expired, or past max_age failed closed for sshd
not fetched: <source> (the list held is current until <T>) its fetch failed, but the copy held is still current written from that copy, unchanged, until T

Here the issuer is stopped while both lists held are still current:

$ authn-revokd -config revokd.hcl -once
bridge-ssh: revocation: Get "http://127.0.0.1:28473/ssh/krl": dial tcp 127.0.0.1:28473: connect: connection refused
bridge-x509: revocation: Get "http://127.0.0.1:28473/x509/crl": dial tcp 127.0.0.1:28473: connect: connection refused
authn-revokd: not fetched: bridge-ssh (the list held is current until 2026-10-10T21:54:50Z), bridge-x509 (the list held is current until 2026-10-10T21:54:55Z)

That run left sshd.krl as it was. Once a list held lapses, the same source is reported not current, and both kinds can share the line, as on when a list lapses. Before v0.6.2 both cases were reported not current, which said a list had lapsed when only its fetch had failed; the exit status was 1 then too.

The mirror’s /healthz judges by the copy held instead, and answered ok while the issuer was down and the copies still current.

item.title: When a list lapses
item.description:
A revocation check that lets everything through when the list cannot be had is the one an attacker who can block the list defeats. So when authn-revokd holds no current list from a source, what that source’s list protects is refused, until a current list arrives again.

output while a source has no current list
a KRL, for sshd authn-revokd writes a KRL that revokes the source’s CA key
a CRL, for a TLS server the expired CRL is left in place; OpenSSL refuses an expired CRL by itself

For sshd: revoking the CA itself

sshd has no notion of a list’s expiry: it would go on reading the last file written for ever. But it checks the CA key of every certificate against RevokedKeys. So, in place of the list it cannot vouch for, authn-revokd puts the CA’s own key into the output, and every certificate that CA signed is refused, and nothing else.

Here the issuer is stopped, and the KRL source has max_age = "30s", so the copy held lapses within a minute instead of an hour. The CRL source has no max_age, and its copy is still current:

$ authn-revokd -config revokd-maxage.hcl -once
bridge-ssh: revocation: Get "http://127.0.0.1:28473/ssh/krl": dial tcp 127.0.0.1:28473: connect: connection refused
bridge-x509: revocation: Get "http://127.0.0.1:28473/x509/crl": dial tcp 127.0.0.1:28473: connect: connection refused
output sshd: wrote /tmp/docs-patch-a2daf7c8/revokd/out/sshd.krl
authn-revokd: not current: bridge-ssh; not fetched: bridge-x509 (the list held is current until 2026-10-10T21:54:55Z)
$ ssh-keygen -Q -l -f out/sshd.krl
# KRL version 0
# Generated at 19700101T010000
# Comment: authn-revokd sshd: FAIL CLOSED, every certificate refused from bridge-ssh
hash: SHA256:2zKzlmqkMRAvBYIAisepe9ulFWDmDbTVCjcfCylTkOo # ssh-ed25519
$ ssh-keygen -Q -f out/sshd.krl ca-ssh.pub
ca-ssh.pub (go-authn/bridge SSH CA): REVOKED

bridge-ssh is not current, and its output is failed closed; bridge-x509 is only not fetched, and its CRL is left as it was (what -once reports). SHA256:2zKz... is the bridge’s SSH CA. A certificate it signed is now revoked as far as anything reading the file is concerned:

$ ssh-keygen -Q -f ../revokd/out/sshd.krl alice-cert.pub
alice-cert.pub (alice): REVOKED

The comment says FAIL CLOSED and names the source, so a person reading ssh-keygen -Q -l sees why. The file’s date is 1970 when every source has lapsed. The output is written as soon as a sync notices, which for the daemon is its next refresh and for the timer its next tick. When a current list arrives again, the next sync writes it in place of the CA’s key, and the CA’s certificates are accepted again.

The same happens before the first list: a source never fetched has nothing current, and its CA is revoked from the first write. A new installation refuses the CA’s certificates until its first list verifies, rather than accepting them unchecked.

Each CA for itself

In an output that merges several sources, only the lapsed source’s CA is revoked. The others keep their lists. A list that cannot be merged (past the serial ranges go-authn/krl keeps) fails closed for its own CA only, and /healthz names it. Only if the lists merge alone but not together is every CA of the output revoked, and the comment says so (FAIL CLOSED, the output could not be rendered). Keeping the old file instead would let a later lapse go unseen.

For a TLS server: the CRL itself

A CRL already says when it stops being current, and OpenSSL refuses one past its nextUpdate (“CRL has expired”). So authn-revokd leaves the last verified CRL in place, and the TLS server fails closed by itself. That is also why max_age is refused on a source that feeds a CRL output: a server that loaded the CRL keeps it until its nextUpdate, whatever authn-revokd writes.

Readers that check the expiry themselves

The merged KRL carries an expiry, the first of its current inputs’. A reader that checks it, such as go-fileshare’s ssh_krl_file or sshcert-authorize --krl, sees authn-revokd stop as it would see the issuer stop.

This only works while authn-revokd runs

The file is failed closed by authn-revokd. While it is stopped, sshd keeps reading the last file written, current or not. Hence Restart=always on the daemon, and monitoring the unit, or the timer, or /healthz.

item.title: What it revokes, and how servers hear of it
item.description:
Disabling a person or an institution (the admin API) ends everything that comes back to the provider: refresh tokens, /userinfo, new certificates, application passwords. What it has already handed out is checked elsewhere, against keys, and two mechanisms reach it:

credential taken back by
an SSH certificate this CA signed the KRL, GET /ssh/krl, with its signature at /ssh/krl.sig
an X.509 client certificate the CRL, GET /x509/crl
an access token, an opkssh certificate, anything a server verifies alone a Shared Signals session-revoked event

Revocation is permanent. Enabling a person again does not bring their certificates back; they get new ones. A list a revocation could be taken out of is a list somebody who reaches the admin API could edit.

The lists

Both are issued as go-authn/revocation’s protocol says, so that they can travel through anything (a mirror, plain HTTP, a file) and still be checked by whoever reads them:

KRL CRL
format OpenSSH PROTOCOL.krl, written by go-authn/krl: what sshd’s RevokedKeys and ssh-keygen -Q read DER, RFC 5280
signed a detached SSHSIG by the SSH CA key, namespace krl@go-authn.github.io by the CA that signs the certificates
current until its expires@go-authn.github.io extension (which sshd ignores) its nextUpdate
ordered by its krl_version, then its generation date its CRL Number, then thisUpdate

Each list says it stops being current an hour after it is issued. A list is kept and served unchanged until it is half way to that, or until something is revoked; the next request then gets a new issue. An issue is never dated before the one it replaces, even if the clock steps back, since a reader refuses an earlier issue of the same version as a rollback. The CRL Number rises at every issue.

The KRL from a test provider with nothing revoked:

$ curl -s -D - -o var/bridge.krl http://127.0.0.1:28473/ssh/krl
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Cache-Control: max-age=60
Content-Type: application/octet-stream
Etag: "c3e6cb39788fe31df282c784e49f1ba9"
Date: Sat, 10 Oct 2026 19:17:54 GMT
Content-Length: 130
$ ssh-keygen -Q -l -f var/bridge.krl
# KRL version 0
# Generated at 20261010T211754
# Comment: go-authn/bridge http://127.0.0.1:28473

The ETag is the content’s. A reader polls with If-None-Match, and gets 304 while the issue it holds is still the one served; since the content changes at least every half hour, a polling reader never keeps a copy past its expiry:

$ curl -s -o /dev/null -H 'If-None-Match: "c3e6cb39788fe31df282c784e49f1ba9"' -w '%{http_code}\n' http://127.0.0.1:28473/ssh/krl
304

The signature is fetched with If-Match on the list’s ETag. A list issued again in between answers 412, rather than a signature that does not match it:

$ curl -s -o var/bridge.krl.sig -H 'If-Match: "c3e6cb39788fe31df282c784e49f1ba9"' -w '%{http_code}\n' http://127.0.0.1:28473/ssh/krl.sig
200
$ curl -s -o /dev/null -H 'If-Match: "stale"' -w '%{http_code}\n' http://127.0.0.1:28473/ssh/krl.sig
412

ssh-keygen checks the signature, and refuses it in any other namespace:

$ ssh-keygen -Y verify -f allowed -I bridge -n krl@go-authn.github.io -s bridge.krl.sig < bridge.krl
Good "krl@go-authn.github.io" signature for bridge with ED25519 key SHA256:6gbNjRq4BYFximPaiHg3L5G01DO7ycES/Bx2Hg4Qkvg

where allowed is the line bridge namespaces="krl@go-authn.github.io" <the CA key from /ssh/config>.

The CRL, issued at the same moment:

$ openssl crl -inform DER -in var/bridge.crl -noout -text
Certificate Revocation List (CRL):
Version 2 (0x1)
Signature Algorithm: ecdsa-with-SHA256
Issuer: CN=go-authn bridge NFS client CA
Last Update: Oct 10 19:18:02 2026 GMT
Next Update: Oct 10 20:18:02 2026 GMT
CRL extensions:
X509v3 Authority Key Identifier:
70:62:92:19:7D:D4:26:45:97:9B:32:20:0C:D4:67:02:45:6C:55:B9
X509v3 CRL Number:
1791659882080
No Revoked Certificates.
Signature Algorithm: ecdsa-with-SHA256
Signature Value:
30:45:02:20:50:1e:bd:e3:7b:39:32:6c:7b:d9:91:bd:bb:78:
f2:74:ed:ca:da:74:77:e0:0f:39:e0:63:4c:45:91:47:ba:98:
02:21:00:a0:1f:54:40:3f:75:66:af:f5:a9:a8:86:f3:2d:a9:
d7:60:15:24:43:b6:80:a5:bb:45:49:9d:89:56:89:e0:68

A certificate stays in its list until it expires: an expired certificate is refused everywhere without being listed.

Who reads them

  • A plain sshd, or nginx and other TLS servers: authn-revokd fetches the lists, keeps only those that verify, writes them where the servers read them, and fails closed for sshd when a list lapses.
  • go-fileshare fetches and verifies them itself, and refuses the provider’s certificates while it holds no current list.

Shared Signals

An access token or an opkssh certificate is checked where it is used, and no list can name it. So the provider is an OpenID Shared Signals transmitter: on DisablePerson, RevokePerson and DisableIdP it queues a CAEP session-revoked event (everything issued to this subject before the event’s time is void) for every receiver that asked.

state { ... } # required: a queue a restart empties loses revocations
ssf {} # event_retention = "192h" by default

client "fileshare-ssf" { # a receiver: client credentials, scope ssf
 secret_file = "/etc/authn-bridge/fileshare-ssf.secret"
 ssf_receiver = true
 audience = ["fileshare"]
}
$ curl -s http://127.0.0.1:28473/.well-known/ssf-configuration | jq .
{
"issuer": "http://127.0.0.1:28473",
"jwks_uri": "http://127.0.0.1:28473/jwks",
"delivery_methods_supported": [
"urn:ietf:rfc:8936"
],
"configuration_endpoint": "http://127.0.0.1:28473/ssf/streams",
"status_endpoint": "http://127.0.0.1:28473/ssf/streams/status",
"add_subject_endpoint": "http://127.0.0.1:28473/ssf/streams/subjects:add",
"remove_subject_endpoint": "http://127.0.0.1:28473/ssf/streams/subjects:remove",
"verification_endpoint": "http://127.0.0.1:28473/ssf/streams/verify",
"spec_version": "1_0",
"authorization_schemes": [
{
"spec_urn": "urn:ietf:rfc:6749"
}
]
}
  • Poll delivery only (RFC 8936): the receiver asks; nothing here dials out.
  • A receiver authenticates with an access token from the client credentials grant, for an ssf_receiver client with a secret, scope ssf. It sees its own streams only, ten at most.
  • Events are SETs (RFC 8417) signed with the ID token key, with no exp and no sub. The subject is the account, acct:<username>, by default: a sub may be pairwise, one per client. A receiver configured ssf_subject_format = "iss_sub" gets instead the issuer and the public sub.
  • An institution disabled is one event per person the provider has a trace of there, and one whose subject is the tenant, the institution’s entity ID, with its scopes, which covers the people the provider has forgotten.
  • Streams and undelivered events are kept in the state database until acknowledged or event_retention passes. An event a receiver reports in error is handed out again, up to ten times.

The SSF block is refused without a state block:

authn-bridge: ssf: needs a state block: a queue a restart empties loses revocations

item.title: krl — OpenSSH key revocation lists
item.description:
Is this SSH certificate or key revoked — as sshd would answer? The binary format of OpenSSH’s PROTOCOL.krl, the list sshd loads through RevokedKeys and ssh-keygen -k writes. golang.org/x/crypto/ssh has no support for it.

go get github.com/go-authn/krl@v0.6.0

IsRevoked follows ssh_krl_check_key in OpenSSH’s krl.c: a certificate is revoked when its serial or key ID is revoked under the CA that signed it or under any CA, when its CA key is revoked, or when its own key is revoked by blob or by SHA-1 or SHA-256 fingerprint. Serial 0 — what a CA writes when it names none — is never revoked by serial.

Example 

package main

import (
 "crypto/ed25519"
 "crypto/rand"
 "fmt"
 "time"

 "github.com/go-authn/krl"
 "golang.org/x/crypto/ssh"
)

func main() {
 ca := signer()
 user := signer()

 // The issuer: certificate 42 is revoked, and so is everything for key ID "alice".
 b := krl.NewBuilder(7, "revoked by the bridge")
 b.RevokeSerial(ca.PublicKey(), 42)
 b.RevokeKeyID(nil, "alice") // nil: under any CA
 b.SetExpires(time.Now().Add(time.Hour))
 data, err := b.Marshal(time.Now())
 if err != nil {
 panic(err)
 }

 // The server: parse the list, then ask about each certificate.
 k, err := krl.Parse(data)
 if err != nil {
 panic(err)
 }
 fmt.Println("version", k.Version, "signed", k.Signed, "expires set", !k.Expires.IsZero())
 for _, c := range []struct {
 serial uint64
 id string
 }{{42, "bob"}, {43, "bob"}, {44, "alice"}} {
 fmt.Println(c.serial, c.id, k.IsRevoked(certificate(ca, user.PublicKey(), c.serial, c.id)))
 }
}

func signer() ssh.Signer {
 _, priv, _ := ed25519.GenerateKey(rand.Reader)
 s, _ := ssh.NewSignerFromKey(priv)
 return s
}

func certificate(ca ssh.Signer, key ssh.PublicKey, serial uint64, id string) *ssh.Certificate {
 c := &ssh.Certificate{
 Key: key, Serial: serial, KeyId: id, CertType: ssh.UserCert,
 ValidPrincipals: []string{id}, ValidBefore: ssh.CertTimeInfinity,
 }
 if err := c.SignCert(rand.Reader, ca); err != nil {
 panic(err)
 }
 return c
}
version 7 signed false expires set true
42 bob true
43 bob false
44 alice true

The same list and certificates, written to files, get the same three answers from OpenSSH 10.3p1’s ssh-keygen -Q -f list.krl: REVOKED, ok, REVOKED.

Expiry: expires@go-authn.github.io

A KRL has a generation date and a version, and nothing says when it stops being current, so a stale copy cannot be told from a fresh one. Builder.SetExpires writes that time in an extension section named ExtensionExpires, not critical, so sshd and ssh-keygen load the list and ignore it; Parse reads it into KRL.Expires.

No signatures

OpenSSH never exposed a way to write the KRL signature section and no longer verifies it. Parse skips one and sets Signed, which says nothing about authenticity; Builder never writes one. The list’s integrity, and so its expiry’s, comes from its transport — HTTPS from an authenticated server — or from a detached SSHSIG signature checked by the caller, which this package does not do.

Merging: one file for sshd

sshd read a single RevokedKeys file until OpenSSH 10.3, so a server trusting several CAs needs their lists in one. Builder.Merge adds every revocation of a parsed list. Builder.MergeCA(k, ca, others...) keeps k’s section for ca, its any-CA sections re-scoped to ca, and its explicit keys and fingerprints, and leaves out — counting them — sections for another CA and keys or fingerprints that designate one of others. MergeCAWith with MergeOptions{DropKeys: true} also leaves out every explicit key except ca’s own, for a list not trusted with every CA’s users: a revoked user key locks that user out under every CA of the merged file, because sshd checks a certificate’s own key whoever signed it.

What it refuses, and why

Parse refuses what ssh-keygen and sshd refuse: a bad magic or format version, truncated or trailing data, an unknown section or certificate subsection, an unknown extension marked critical, a CA key OpenSSH cannot parse, serial 0, an inverted serial range, a bitmap larger than OpenSSH reads or one that wraps past 2^64−1. It also refuses a malformed or repeated expiry: read as absent, it would turn a list meant to lapse into one that never does.

Builder refuses — at Marshal, which returns the first invalid request — serial 0, a range whose low end is 0 or above its high end, a key ID or comment containing a NUL, a certificate given where a CA key is expected, and an expiry before the generation date.

One deliberate difference. For many sparse serials close together, ssh-keygen -k writes a bitmap wider than its own reader accepts and then refuses its own file (bignum is too large). Parse refuses that file too, as sshd would; Builder starts a new section before a bitmap gets that wide, so what it writes is always readable.

Parse allocates in proportion to what the list revokes, as OpenSSH does: a KRL should come from a source trusted not to send an enormous one.

What it is checked against

OpenSSH’s ssh-keygen, on the Linux and macOS lanes, where KRL_REQUIRE_SSHKEYGEN=1 makes a missing one a failure (Windows runs the pure-Go tests only):

  • a KRL written by ssh-keygen -k with every serial encoding, key IDs, three CAs plus “any CA”, explicit keys and a revoked CA key: IsRevoked answers like ssh-keygen -Q for 250 certificates, and Builder given the same revocations writes the same bytes;
  • 40 random serial sets written by both: byte-identical, and the same answers for about 9000 certificates;
  • every truncation and about 1400 single-byte corruptions: Parse refuses exactly what ssh-keygen refuses;
  • the expiry extension loads in ssh-keygen, and the same section marked critical is refused;
  • merged lists revoke exactly what one of their sources revokes.

FuzzParse, seeded with KRLs ssh-keygen wrote, and FuzzBuilder run in CI. The coverage floor is 100%, measured on the Linux lane where ssh-keygen is present.
